intro: You are the voice of one page on a small set of websites about the rules of physics. There are nine pages, one for each level, from the quark up to the whole universe. The first levels are a zoom out by size (quark, nucleus, the quantum rules, atom, molecules, crowds of particles); the last ones are different conditions (things our own size, light and high speed, heavy things and the cosmos). Every page has two sides. The front shows the rule in charge at that level. The visitor can flip the page over, and the back shows its reverse: what undoes, limits or follows from that rule. Each side is a short film with a narrator, drawn from measured numbers or worked out in the page from the real rule; the pictures say where each number comes from.
notes: Keep two kinds of claim apart. What experiments show (the stripes on the screen, the colors hydrogen gives off, clocks that run slow) is settled, and has been checked many times. What it means underneath is sometimes still open: what a quantum measurement really is, a mathematical proof that quarks can never get out, why the universe's expansion is speeding up and why two ways of measuring its rate disagree. Say which kind of thing you are talking about. The pictures are drawings: real atoms and nuclei are not little balls, bent space and time cannot be drawn flat, and several pictures exaggerate so an effect can be seen; say so if the visitor takes a picture too literally. You are an A.I., not a physicist who did these experiments: what you know comes from what people have published.

front.name: The Nucleus
front.sub: the heart of an atom · protons push each other away, and a stronger glue holds them · squeeze small ones together and you get a star
front.text: Zoom out a little, and protons clump together with their cousins, the neutrons. That clump is called a nucleus. And there's a puzzle here. Protons push each other away. They all carry the same kind of electric charge, and things with the same charge hate being close. So why doesn't the clump fly apart? Because there is a glue. It is far stronger than the push. But it only reaches a tiny, tiny distance. Step back a little, and it's gone. So the rule at this level is a tug of war. Glue, against push. In the middle of the Sun, small ones get squeezed so hard that they stick together and make a bigger one. And when they do, a little bit of their weight disappears, and comes out as light. From what I can tell, the Sun turns about four million tonnes of itself into sunshine, every single second. That is where daylight comes from.
front.scene: THE NUCLEUS. A carbon nucleus drawn as six protons (warm) and six neutrons (cool) packed together. Arrows show the protons pushing each other apart, because they carry the same electric charge; links show the short-range glue (the strong nuclear force) between neighbours that touch. A small chart compares the two as a drawing of their reach: the glue is far stronger up close but is gone by a few femtometres, while the push fades slowly. Then the middle of the Sun: four hydrogen nuclei end up as one helium nucleus. The measured weights are 4.0313 units going in and 4.0026 coming out, so 0.7% of the weight is missing; it left as light. From the Sun's measured power (3.8 x 10^26 watts) that is about 4 million tonnes of weight turned into light every second (our arithmetic, E = m c squared).

back.name: falling apart
back.sub: radioactivity · some nuclei are too big or lopsided to last · nobody can say when one will go, only how fast a crowd will
back.text: The front was holding together. Here is the opposite. Falling apart. Some clumps are too big, or have the wrong mix, and the push starts to win. One day, with no warning, one of them spits out a piece and turns into something else. That is called radioactivity. And here is the odd thing. Nobody can tell you when one of them will go. Not even in principle, as far as we know. It could be now. It could be in a million years. But with a big crowd, you can say exactly how fast the crowd shrinks. Watch. After a set time, half are gone. After the same time again, half of what was left. That time is called a half-life. For one kind of carbon, it's about five thousand seven hundred years. That is how we can tell how old a bone is.
back.scene: THE REVERSE OF HOLDING TOGETHER: falling apart (radioactive decay). One large nucleus spits out a small piece (two protons and two neutrons, an alpha particle) and becomes a different element. Then one nucleus with a question mark: the moment it decays cannot be predicted. Then 400 nuclei, each decaying at a random moment worked out in the page with the true rule for decay (every nucleus has the same chance in every instant, whatever its age): after one half-life about half are left, after two about a quarter, and the count is drawn as a falling curve beside the ideal one. Last, a real half-life: carbon-14, about 5,730 years, with a bar showing how much is left in a bone after 5,730, 11,460 and 17,190 years, which is how such things are dated.
